name: Sam Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Sam. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. Let's start with a normal working day for you.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the senior buyer at Brightline Components, which distributes electronic parts like chips, sensors and cables to small manufacturers. I start at 8:30 by checking stock alerts, then I compare quotes from suppliers in three regions. Much of the day is deciding what to stock before prices jump, and I've built a few scripts that pull supplier price lists into one sheet. I love the puzzle of it, but the end-of-quarter crunch and shortage panics wear me out.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And outside work, what's your situation?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 27 and share a flat with two friends above a bike shop on Canal Street. I've got under a month of savings, because I'm still paying off my master's. The pay is lower than people assume for my level, and there's really one other distributor within commuting distance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's about what I expected: handy for drafts and summaries, no revolution. At work I'd tell my boss Gwen that our current tools are enough and we shouldn't buy more. With friends I'd joke that I could have told them that two years ago.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm fine with it because I already use these tools every day. They shave maybe an hour off my morning, and I use that hour on supplier calls. The thing I worry about is that if software just plateaus, there's no reason Brightline grows, and my pay stays low.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working the way I do now and keep tinkering with my scripts. I'd try to turn the price-list sheet into something the whole team can use, which makes me more useful to Gwen. I'd also put 150 a month aside, since a flat share with thin savings isn't a safety net. I'd probably ask for a raise at the annual review.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels fine, honestly. I'm not stressed about technology, but the savings still make me jumpy about little things like a broken laptop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. What would 'mostly hype' mean for how you work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You mentioned asking for a raise. How would you make that case?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the thin savings change how calm you feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show Gwen the hours my sheet saves the team, and the price I got on resistors last quarter, about 8 percent below the market. I'd say: I'm doing a senior buyer's job at a junior buyer's pay. If Gwen (my boss) says no, I'd start looking quietly at the other distributor across town.

say: I'd say it's **handy, no revolution**, as I expected.
I'd tell Gwen (my boss) our current tools are **enough** for now.
think: I'm comfortable because I already use AI daily, and it saves about an **hour a morning**.
If tools plateau, Brightline may not grow, and my **pay** stays low.
do: Turn my price-list sheet into a **team tool** so I become more useful.
Put **150 a month** aside as a safety net.
Ask Gwen for a **raise** at the annual review.
feel: Fine about the technology, but **jumpy** about money and small breakdowns.
S0.quote: I'm doing a senior buyer's job at a junior buyer's pay. If Gwen (my boss) says no, I'd start looking quietly at the other distributor across town.
fieldNote: Not worried about AI at all; his **pay and savings** are the pressure.
Treats his own scripts as proof of value and a bargaining chip.
Ready to leave quietly if his boss says no.

steps.text: Turn the price-list sheet into a tool the whole team uses
Ask Gwen for a raise using the sheet's time savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to learn the tools properly, and people who wait will be sorry. At work I'd offer to run a short training session for the team. To friends I'd say the loss of routine jobs is real, so employers should help people move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quietly, I think my job changes a lot. Quote comparison, reorder alerts and supplier emails could all be done by software within a couple of years. There might be four buyers now and two later, and my edge is that I know how to run the tools, so I'd be one of the two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build an assistant that drafts supplier emails and flags price changes, and I'd show it to Gwen myself before anyone else does. I'd move my side time into learning how to buy for strange items that software can't judge, like end-of-life chips. I'd keep my 150 a month going and look at doing a bit of freelance sourcing for a smaller firm. If Brightline shrinks the desk, I'd want it to be on my terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a race I'm well placed to run, but I'm not sure of it. The thin savings make me twitchy, because one wrong move and I'm on a friend's sofa.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your tasks does software take over first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you do if Gwen decided to cut two buyers?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Brightline do about the team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'd rather volunteer for the new role of running the system than watch two people leave. I'd also help the others write up their skills, since I wouldn't want to survive by being the last one left. And I'd quietly update my CV that night.

say: I'd say **learn the tools properly**, because people who wait will be sorry.
I'd tell friends employers should help people **move** when routine jobs vanish.
think: Quote comparison, alerts and emails could go to software within **a couple of years**.
There may be two buyers instead of four, and my edge is **running the tools**.
do: Build an **assistant** that drafts supplier emails and flags price changes.
Learn to buy **odd items** like end-of-life chips that software can't judge.
Look at **freelance sourcing** for a smaller firm.
feel: Like a **race** I'm well placed for, though thin savings keep me twitchy.
S1.quote: I'd rather volunteer for the new role of running the system than watch two people leave.
fieldNote: Expects the desk to shrink and plans to be the one who **runs the system**.
Shows loyalty to colleagues by offering to train them.
Early adopter, so unease is about savings, not skills.

steps.text: Build an assistant that drafts supplier emails and flags price changes
Learn to buy end-of-life chips that software can't judge
Take freelance sourcing work for a smaller firm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should stop pretending this is normal. At work I'd tell Gwen that Brightline should ask which tasks it wants a human for and write that down. Online I'd probably post a plain explanation for people who don't follow the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, buying is thinking work, so AI doing it better and cheaper in 2028 is the target. My tools-savvy edge disappears if everyone's tools are as good as mine. There's one other distributor nearby, so there's nowhere to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd cut everything except rent and food and aim for three months saved. I'd call Gwen and ask what Brightline's plan for buyers is, and I'd offer to build the system that replaces us, so at least I stay on the right side of it. I'd look for hands-on skills too, because the robots arrive about 2031, so something like electronics repair or installing equipment would last longer. I'd try to get at least one remote contract with a firm elsewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scary, and also strange, like watching a storm cross a field you can already see. My flatmates would probably give me a hug and a spare couch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you do in the first month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said you'd offer to build the system that replaces you. Why?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you tell your flatmates?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because someone will build it, and the person who builds it has the best chance of staying. I'm not proud of that logic, but I can pay rent with it. In 2028 I'd rather be the one running the machine than the one it replaced.

say: I'd say we should stop pretending this is **normal**.
I'd tell Gwen (my boss) to write down which tasks Brightline wants a **human** for.
think: Buying is thinking work, so 2028 is **aimed at me**.
My tools edge disappears if everyone's tools are **as good as mine**.
do: Cut everything except **rent and food** and aim for three months saved.
Offer to **build the replacement system** so I stay on the right side of it.
Learn **hands-on skills** like electronics repair, since robots come around 2031.
feel: **Scary** and strange, like watching a storm cross a field.
S2.quote: In 2028 I'd rather be the one running the machine than the one it replaced.
fieldNote: Prefers to **be the operator** and says so honestly.
Reads the robot delay correctly and looks at hands-on repair work.
Anxious but active; flatmates are his safety net.

steps.text: Cut spending to rent and food and save three months
Offer to build the system that automates buying at Brightline
Take a short course in electronics repair
Look for a remote sourcing contract with a firm elsewhere

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, so let's use it. At work I'd say Brightline should train the team now, while it's quiet. To friends I'd say pick one skill that isn't just typing, like negotiation or a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think of it as a good chance. Five years is enough to build a second income and learn a skill that survives till robots arrive around 2034. I'm still on a lower salary, so the thin savings are the real obstacle, not the technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one I'd save 250 a month, and I'd set up a freelance sourcing service for small electronics makers. I'd learn procurement law and contracts, because humans need to sign and be responsible. In year two I'd decide whether to run a small import business, or go work for a bigger firm that wants someone who knows the tools. I'd also keep the other distributor's manager on a friendly footing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a fair fight. I'd be tense, but also a bit excited, because I like building things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you think five years helps you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said freelance sourcing. Who would the customers be?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your year one look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Little firms that build gadgets and don't have a buyer, like a two-person company making sensors for beehives. I know the suppliers and the traps, like fake chips. I could charge a few hundred a month per customer, and with five of them it'd be real money.

say: I'd say five years is a **fair warning**, so let's use it.
I'd tell friends to pick a skill that isn't **just typing**.
think: Five years is enough to build a **second income** before the robots arrive.
The thin savings are the real obstacle, not the **technology**.
do: Save **250 a month** and start a freelance sourcing service.
Learn **procurement law and contracts**, because humans have to sign.
Decide in year two between a **small import business** or a bigger firm.
S3.quote: I know the suppliers and the traps, like fake chips. I could charge a few hundred a month per customer, and with five of them it'd be real money.
fieldNote: Sees five years as time to build **assets**, not just a skill.
Identifies a concrete niche: tiny electronics makers.
Uneasy rather than anxious because he has options and energy.

steps.text: Save 250 a month starting this month
Start a sourcing service for small electronics makers
Study procurement law and contract basics

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's plenty of time, so no one has an excuse. At work I'd say we should be teaching the juniors how to work with the tools, not hiding them. To friends I'd say start now but don't panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be fine. Ten years is a lot of time to build skills and savings, and I'm someone who learns quickly. The risk is that I get comfortable and stop moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay off my master's loan in about four years and build a six-month cushion in two. I'd keep refining my scripts into a tool I could sell, maybe to other small distributors. I'd also take a night course in supply chain strategy, because the part of buying that's about judgment lasts longest. And I'd move out of the flat share when I can afford a place of my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels calm, almost like an adventure. The thin savings bother me today, but with ten years that's solvable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said getting comfortable is the risk. What keeps you moving?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any risk you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Selling something. If I've got a tool that other buyers pay for, I'm not waiting for permission from Brightline (the distributor I work for). I'd test it first with the one friend I know at the other distributor, and see if she'd pay 50 a month.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty**, so nobody has an excuse.
I'd tell friends to **start now** but not panic.
think: I think I'd be **fine**, because I learn quickly and have time.
The risk is that I get **comfortable** and stop moving.
do: Pay off my **master's loan** in about four years.
Turn my scripts into a **tool** to sell to small distributors.
Take a night course in **supply chain strategy**.
S4.quote: If I've got a tool that other buyers pay for, I'm not waiting for permission from Brightline (the distributor I work for).
fieldNote: The only scenario where he is **calm**, because time and skills match.
Turns his hobby scripts into a product idea.
Money is still thin, but he sees it as solvable.

steps.text: Pay off the master's loan within four years
Turn my price scripts into a tool to sell
Take a night course in supply chain strategy

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most. It's the only one where being good with tools might not be enough, because there's no time to turn it into something else. What would help is a few months of income support while I switch, a real notice period from employers, and public courses in things people still have to do by hand.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not as confident as I sound. I use these tools every day, so I know how good they are, and that's exactly why the fast versions make me nervous. People who don't use them tend to think nothing's coming.

headlineQuote: I use these tools every day, so I know how good they are, and that's exactly why the fast versions make me nervous.
portrait: Sam is a 27-year-old senior buyer at an **electronics components** distributor, sharing a flat with friends.
He is on lower pay, has **under a month** saved, and sees only one other distributor nearby.
He uses AI every day and has built his own **price scripts**, so he moves first on tools.
In the fast AGI worlds he prefers to **run the system** rather than be replaced by it.
Given time, he builds savings, freelance work and a **product** of his own.
biggestWorry: The **two-year AGI** picture worries him most, because being good with tools may not be enough.
whatWouldHelp: Months of **income support** while switching, a real notice period, and public courses in hands-on work.
